title: Biblical Womanhood: A Bible Study on Women of Valor
subtitle: A five-session study on womanhood, calling, and the image of God.
summary:
This study is for women who have wondered whether the church actually believes what Genesis says about them, for the men who have quietly assumed it was written for them, and for the small groups willing to read the whole canon instead of the same three verses. It walks slowly through five sessions, beginning with the dignity Genesis 1 gives every woman as the image of God and the way the fall distorted that dignity into rivalry and rule. It recovers the women the church forgot to teach, Deborah who judged Israel, Huldah who authenticated the word of God, Junia counted among the apostles, Phoebe who carried the letter to the Romans, Priscilla who corrected a preacher, Mary Magdalene sent to tell the men that Christ was alive. It takes the eshet chayil of Proverbs 31 back from the checklist it became and returns her to what the Hebrew says, a woman of valor, a warrior word. It reads the hard texts, First Timothy 2 and First Corinthians 14, and sets the complementarian and egalitarian readings side by side, each in its strongest form, before it lands. And it ends on calling in every season, single, married, mother, widow, worker, refusing to reduce a woman's worth to any one of them.

This is not a study written down to women from a safe height. It is written by a man, a pastor, a husband, the father of five sons, who has to confess at the outset that men built much of the church for men, that the sermons he grew up on quoted Paul's hard sentences to women and skipped the women Paul honored by name, that he himself has taught rooms as if half of them were furniture. He writes from inside that failure, not above it. And on the contested questions of what women may do in the church, the study refuses the cheap win in either direction. It states the complementarian case and the egalitarian case each the way its own best defenders would state it, sorts the matter honestly by how much it binds, and names where the author lands and the strongest objection he has not fully answered. A woman on the other side of that question should finish feeling understood, not beaten. The dignity is not up for a vote. The rest is held with an open hand.
audience: Women, the men who worship beside them, and mixed or women's small groups

sessions.title: Made in the Image of God
sessions.aim: To ground a woman's worth not in her usefulness, her beauty, her marital status, or her fruitfulness but in the bare fact that Genesis 1 makes her the image of God, and to trace how the fall distorted that equal dignity into rule and rivalry so that the distortion is never mistaken for the design.
sessions.summary: A woman told Bell, after a lifetime in church, that she had learned to think of herself as a supporting character in someone else's story, useful to a husband, a family, a ministry, and worth exactly what she produced for them. She was not bitter. She was reporting what she had been taught, and much of it she had been taught in a sanctuary. The real question is not whether women matter, everyone will say they do, but on what ground they matter, because a worth grounded in usefulness can be revoked the moment the usefulness runs out. Genesis 1 grounds it somewhere the usefulness cannot reach. God creates humanity in his own image, and then the text says the thing the church keeps forgetting to say out loud, male and female he created them, both, equally, the image of God stamped on the woman as fully as on the man before either has done a single useful thing. Then Genesis 2 calls her ezer, helper, and Bell takes the strong case that helper means subordinate, the assistant, the second, because that is how the word landed on many of us. He grants why it sounds that way. But the same Hebrew word is used most often in the Old Testament of God himself, the ezer of Israel, which is not the language of a subordinate but of a rescuer, so the woman is not the man's assistant, she is his necessary strength. Then the fall, and the distortion. God tells the woman that her desire will be for her husband and he will rule over her, and Bell insists this is a description of the wreckage, not a prescription for the design. The rule of man over woman is a symptom of the curse, not a command within it. The image was equal in the garden. The domination came in with the thorns.

keyScripture.why: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him, male and female he created them, naming the woman as fully the image of God as the man, the ground of a dignity that no role, season, or usefulness confers and none can revoke.

discussion.q: Bell says many women were taught to see themselves as supporting characters, worth what they produce for a husband, a family, a ministry. Where have you absorbed a worth grounded in usefulness rather than in the image of God?
discussion.behind: Open on the felt ground before the theological one. Most women in the room can name a place where their value felt conditional, tied to what they gave. The aim is to expose the conditional worth honestly before Genesis 1 answers it. Let it land on recognition, not yet on the fix, and let the men in the room hear how common this is.

discussion.q: Genesis 1 says male and female he created them, both the image of God, before either has done anything useful. What changes when you hear that your worth was settled before your usefulness began?
discussion.behind: This is the theological center of the session. The image is conferred at creation, not earned by contribution, which means it cannot be revoked by failure or age or singleness or an empty womb. Do not let it drift into a general self-esteem message. The ground is God's own image, not the woman's feelings about herself. The relief is that the verdict was in before the performance started.

discussion.q: The word Genesis uses for the woman, ezer, helper, is used most often of God himself, the helper of Israel. How does that reframe a word many of us heard as subordinate?
discussion.behind: Repair a word that has done damage. Many in the room heard helper as assistant, the second, the lesser. The text uses the same word of God, who is no one's subordinate. Help the room feel that ezer names necessary strength, a rescuer, not a sidekick. Do not overcorrect into erasing distinction, just recover the dignity the word actually carries.

discussion.q: Bell says the rule of man over woman in Genesis 3 is a description of the curse, not a prescription for the design. Why does it matter enormously which one it is?
discussion.behind: Press on the difference between description and prescription, because everything downstream depends on it. If male domination is the design, the church should enforce it. If it is the curse, the church should be undoing it, the way it works against every other effect of the fall. Help the room see that treating a symptom of the curse as a command is like blessing the thorns. Keep it careful, this is where the contested questions begin, but they come later.

discussion.q: Bell confesses that men, himself included, have built much of the church as if it were for men, and taught rooms as though half of them were furniture. Where have you seen that, and where have you, whatever your sex, treated a woman as less than the image of God?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication for the whole room, not only the men. The point is not to stage a grievance session against men in absentia, and not to let men perform guilt either. Everyone is inside this, women who have believed the lesser story about themselves, men who have taught it, all of us who have measured a person by her use. Go first and name your own.

objections.objection: The Bible plainly puts men over women from the very start, so all this talk about equal dignity is just reading modern feminism back into an ancient text that never meant it.
objections.response: Take the concern seriously, because it is guarding something real, a refusal to bend Scripture to the spirit of the age, and that instinct is right even when the conclusion is wrong. But look at where the text actually puts the ordering. Genesis 1 gives the image equally, male and female, with no hierarchy in sight, and Genesis 2 calls the woman ezer, a word Scripture uses of God himself. The rule of man over woman does not appear until Genesis 3, after the fall, in the list of things that have gone wrong, alongside pain and thorns and death. That is not modern feminism reading something in. It is simply reading the chapters in order and noticing where the domination enters, which is with the curse and not with the creation. To treat the curse as the blueprint is not high a view of Scripture. It is a low one, mistaking the disease for the design.

objections.objection: If men and women are equal image-bearers, then any distinction between them at all is just oppression, and the honest thing is to erase the difference entirely.
objections.response: Hear the good intention, because it is reacting against centuries of real diminishment, and the anger at that is not sin. But equal worth has never required erased difference, and Genesis will not let us collapse the two. The same passage that grants the woman the full image also says male and female he created them, naming a difference God calls good before the fall ever touches it. The lie is not that men and women differ. The lie is that difference means a ladder, that distinction must mean rank. Genesis refuses both errors at once, the one that turns difference into hierarchy and the one that abolishes difference to secure equality. The woman is fully the image, and she is not simply a man, and both of those are said in the same breath by the same God who called the whole of it very good.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If God settled your worth before you had done a single useful thing, whose verdict have you actually been living under instead, and what would it change to believe his?
sessions.practice: This week, catch yourself once measuring your worth by what you produced, the tasks finished, the people served, the approval earned, and instead of arguing with the feeling, preach the fact to yourself, that you were the image of God before any of it and will be after all of it is gone. Write down what it stirs in you to rest your worth on something you did not earn and cannot lose.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, before we had done anything useful, you made us in your own image, male and female, and called it very good. Forgive us for learning to weigh ourselves by our usefulness, and forgive your church where it taught the daughters of God to think of themselves as supporting characters in someone else's story. Undo in us the rule and rivalry that came in with the curse, and give us back the equal dignity of the garden. Where a woman in this room has never once heard that her worth was settled before her performance began, let her hear it now, and let it hold. Amen.
reflection: Where have I grounded my worth in usefulness, beauty, or role rather than in the image of God, and what happens to that worth when the usefulness runs out?
Have I heard the word helper as subordinate, and how does it change to know Scripture uses it of God the rescuer?
Where have I treated a woman, or myself, as less than the full image of God, mistaking a symptom of the curse for the design?
sessions.teaching: A woman told Bell, near the end of a lifetime spent inside the church, that she had come to think of herself as a supporting character in somebody else's story. Useful to a husband. Useful to her children. Useful to a ministry that needed hands. And worth, she said, about what she produced for them in a given week. She was not angry when she said it. That was the part that stopped him. She was calmly reporting a lesson she had learned, and she had learned a good deal of it in a sanctuary, from people who loved her and would have been horrified to hear it named. So we begin not with a slogan about how much women matter, because everyone in the room will nod at that and nothing will move. We begin with the harder question underneath it, which is on what ground a woman matters, because a worth grounded in usefulness is a worth that can be revoked the moment the usefulness runs out, when the children are grown, when the body ages, when the marriage does not come or does not last, when the hands can no longer do the work. If that is the ground, then every woman is one bad season from worthlessness, and many of them know it, and it sits under a great deal of the exhaustion women carry into church on a Sunday. Genesis 1 puts the ground somewhere the usefulness cannot reach it. God makes humanity in his own image, and then the text says the sentence the church keeps forgetting to read aloud. Male and female he created them. Both. Equally. The image of God stamped on the woman as fully and as early as it is stamped on the man, before either of them has served anyone, borne anyone, earned anything, done a single useful thing. That is not a supporting-character worth. That is the highest dignity the Bible knows how to confer, given to her in the same breath and by the same act as it is given to him. Now watch the second chapter, because this is where a good word got bent. Genesis 2 calls the woman ezer, which our Bibles translate helper, and I have to grant the strong case for hearing that as subordinate, because that is exactly how it landed on many of us. Helper sounds like assistant. It sounds like the second, the lesser, the one who hands the surgeon the instruments. If that is what the word meant, then the woman is defined from the start as an auxiliary to the man, and a great deal of teaching has assumed precisely that. But the teaching almost never mentions this. That same Hebrew word, ezer, is used more often in the Old Testament of God than of anyone else. God is the ezer of Israel, the helper who is their shield and their strength, the one the psalmist looks to for help that comes from the Maker of heaven and earth. That is not the language of a subordinate. It is the language of a rescuer, of necessary strength arriving for someone who cannot make it alone. So the woman is not the man's assistant. She is his ezer kenegdo, a strength that corresponds to him and stands in front of him, and to call that subordinate is to say the same thing about God. Then comes the fall, and with it the distortion we spend the rest of history mistaking for the design. God tells the woman that her desire will be for her husband and that he will rule over her, and everything depends on hearing that sentence correctly. It is not a command. It is a diagnosis. It sits in the middle of a list of things that have gone wrong, right beside pain in childbirth and thorns in the field and dust returning to dust. The rule of man over woman is named there the way cancer is named on a chart, as a thing that has entered and should not be there, not as a treatment plan to be followed. The equal dignity was the garden. The domination came in with the curse. And I have to stand inside this before I say another word to anyone, because men built much of the church I serve in, and we built it for men. I grew up on sermons that could quote Paul's two hard sentences to women from memory and had never once mentioned Deborah or Huldah or Junia or Phoebe. I have stood in front of rooms and taught as though half the people in them were furniture, present but not addressed, there to support the real work rather than to do it. That is not the design of Genesis. It is a symptom of the curse wearing a stole and calling itself order. The gospel does not bless the thorns. It came to pull them out by the root, and it starts by telling a woman who has spent her life as a supporting character that she was the image of God before the story ever needed her for anything, and will be long after it does.

scriptureStudy.note: Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. The image is announced as a plural project, and the humanity it produces is not the man alone but the pair, so the very definition of the image includes the woman from the first sentence.

Male and female he created him. The clause the church forgets to read aloud. The image of God is stamped on the woman as fully as on the man, at creation, before role or usefulness, which means her dignity is conferred and not earned.

God blessed them and said to them, be fruitful and multiply and have dominion. The dominion is given to both, jointly, not to the man to be shared down to the woman. The first commission in Scripture is a partnership, not a hierarchy.

It is not good that the man should be alone, I will make him a helper fit for him. The only thing called not good in a very good creation is a man without the woman, which names her not as an accessory but as the answer to the first lack God declares.

My help comes from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. Ezer, the same word Genesis uses for the woman, is here used of God the helper, which strips the word of any hint of the subordinate and fills it with the sense of a rescuing strength.

Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you. Spoken after the fall, in the list of the curse alongside pain and thorns, this describes the wreckage of the relationship, not the design of it, the domination that entered with sin and was never the blueprint.

There is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus. Paul does not abolish the difference God called good, but he abolishes the ranking the curse introduced, declaring the woman a full and equal heir of everything Christ won, which is the garden dignity restored.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the history the session only gestures at, because the church did not read Genesis in a vacuum and the readings it inherited did real damage worth naming. For long stretches of Christian history influential voices treated the woman as a lesser or derivative image, sometimes drawing on Paul's line about the man being the image and glory of God while forgetting the plain statement of Genesis 1 that the image belongs to male and female together. A group should sit honestly with that record, neither excusing it nor pretending it is the whole story, since the same tradition also produced fierce defenders of women's full dignity and reformers who recovered the Genesis text against the accretions. Set beside this the Hebrew scholarship on ezer kenegdo, the phrase for the woman in Genesis 2, and notice that ezer is a word of strength and rescue used chiefly of God, while kenegdo carries the sense of a counterpart who stands corresponding to and in front of the other, so that the phrase names neither a servant nor a clone but a strength that answers a lack. Then take the harder turn into the deeper anthropology. The image of God is not a possession the human owns but a vocation the human is, a being made to reflect God into the world, and when a culture or a church treats a woman as a means to someone else's end it does not merely wound her feelings, it defaces the image of God in her and impoverishes the reflection God intended the world to receive. Weigh this against the modern instinct to secure a woman's worth by making her self-defining and autonomous, and notice that Scripture secures it by a stronger and stranger claim, that her worth was conferred by God before she could define anything, which no failure and no season can revoke. The aim is not to despise the longing for dignity, which is right, but to see how both an oppressive tradition and an autonomous modern answer miss the ground Genesis actually gives, and to ask where each has crept into the room's own assumptions.
sessions.caseStudy: A woman in your group is capable, tireless, the one every ministry leans on, and she says, half joking, that she is only as good as her last casserole and her last carpool. When the session names worth grounded in usefulness, she laughs it off, insisting she is fine, that she likes being needed, that this is just who she is. Here is the work for the leader, and it must honor her before it presses her. Her service is real and good and too rarely thanked, and you should say so plainly and mean it. But notice the phrase, only as good as, because it is the conditional worth speaking out loud, the image of God quietly renegotiated into a performance review. The danger is not that she serves. It is that the serving has become the thing that earns her the right to exist, so that a season of not being needed would read to her as a loss of worth, which is the opposite of what Genesis says over her. Do not shame her service or tell her to do less. Honor it fully, and still ask her, gently, who she would be to God on the week she produced nothing at all, and whether she can hear that the answer was settled in Genesis 1 before the first casserole was ever baked.

sessions.title: The Women the Church Forgot to Teach
sessions.aim: To recover the women Scripture honors by name and role, Deborah, Huldah, Junia, Phoebe, Priscilla, Mary Magdalene, whom much preaching quietly skipped, and to let the sheer weight of their presence expose how selectively the church has read its own Bible.
sessions.summary: Bell says he could recite Paul's two hard sentences to women before he was ten, and did not learn until he was a grown pastor that Paul had also greeted a woman named Junia and called her, in the same letter, notable among the apostles. The gap was not in the Bible. It was in what he had been handed. The real question is not whether the Bible restricts women, that is session four, but whether the church has read the whole of what its Bible actually says about them, and the honest answer is that for a long time it did not. So this session simply reads the record the sermons skipped. Deborah, a prophetess, judged Israel, and the general would not go to war without her. Huldah, a prophetess, was the one the king's men consulted to authenticate the newly found book of the law, and the reform of a nation ran through her word. Phoebe carried Paul's letter to the Romans and is named a servant, a deacon, of her church. Priscilla, with her husband, took a gifted preacher aside and taught him the way of God more accurately. Mary Magdalene was the first witness of the resurrection and was sent by the risen Christ to tell the men, which the early church called being the apostle to the apostles. Bell takes the strong case that none of this settles the debated questions about office and authority, and he grants it fully, because it does not, and he will not pretend a list of examples is an argument it is not. But it settles something else, and something prior. It settles that God has spoken his word through women, led his people through women, entrusted the first news of the empty tomb to a woman, and that a church which forgot to teach any of that was not being careful with Scripture. It was being careless with half of it.

keyScripture.why: Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners, they are well known to the apostles, and they were in Christ before me, naming a woman among those Paul honors at the highest level, a name much of the church managed not to mention for centuries.

discussion.q: Bell says he could quote Paul's hard sentences to women years before he ever heard the name Junia. Which of these women, Deborah, Huldah, Junia, Phoebe, Priscilla, Mary Magdalene, had you genuinely never been taught, and what does the gap tell you?
discussion.behind: Open by surfacing the omission honestly and without accusation. Most in the room will admit they know the restrictive verses far better than the honored women. The point is not to score against anyone but to notice that the gap is real and to ask who chose the reading list. Let the recognition land before any argument about what it means.

discussion.q: Deborah judged Israel and Huldah authenticated the book of the law, both named prophetesses through whom God spoke and led his people. What does it do to you to know that the word and leadership of God ran through women in the Old Testament?
discussion.behind: Let the Old Testament witnesses carry their own weight. These are not obscure footnotes, they are a judge over the nation and the prophet who launched a reform. Help the room feel the size of it before rushing to reconcile it with anything, because the reconciling instinct often shrinks the women back down. Sit with the fact that God chose them.

discussion.q: Mary Magdalene was the first witness of the resurrection and was sent by Christ himself to tell the men. Why do you think God arranged the most important announcement in history to come first through a woman, in a culture that would not accept a woman's testimony in court?
discussion.behind: Press on the deliberate scandal of it. In a world where a woman's legal testimony was discounted, the risen Christ entrusts the founding news of the faith to women first, which no one inventing a persuasive story would have done. Help the room see both the historical credibility this lends the resurrection and the deliberate honor it confers, and let it sit without being tidied away.

discussion.q: Bell grants plainly that these examples do not by themselves settle the debated questions about office and authority. Why does he refuse to make the list prove more than it does, and why does honesty here matter?
discussion.behind: Guard the intellectual honesty that will earn the room's trust for session four. A pile of examples is not an argument about office, and pretending it is would be the mirror image of the selective reading being critiqued. Help the room see that recovering these women does not require overreaching, and that the refusal to overreach is what makes the recovery credible rather than partisan.

discussion.q: Bell says a church that forgot to teach these women was not being careful with Scripture but careless with half of it. Where have you, or your church, read selectively, and what does it cost to keep doing it?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication for the whole room. Selective reading is not a sin of the distant past or the other tribe, it is a habit everyone practices, keeping the verses that confirm us and skipping the ones that complicate us. The cost is a shrunken Bible and a shrunken church. Go first and name a place you read selectively, and keep it off any single political target.

objections.objection: These are just a handful of exceptions. A few unusual women here and there does not overturn the clear general pattern of male leadership across the whole Bible.
objections.response: Grant the real point inside the objection, because it is not nothing. A list of examples is not a doctrine of office, and this session does not pretend it is, and honesty requires saying that plainly. But watch the move the objection makes, because calling them exceptions is doing a lot of quiet work. When God raises up a woman to judge his people, another to authenticate his word, another to be the first herald of the resurrection, and Paul honors a woman among the apostles and commends another as a deacon, the pattern is not a scattering of anomalies to be explained away. It is a consistent thread the church trained itself not to see. You do not have to conclude anything about office to admit that a Bible read whole includes these women prominently, and that a teaching tradition which never mentioned them was not describing the Bible's pattern but editing it.

objections.objection: You are romanticizing these women to push an agenda. Deborah, for instance, is sometimes read as a rebuke to the men who would not lead, not as an endorsement of women leading.
objections.response: Take the reading seriously, because it is a real interpretation held by serious people and deserves a fair hearing rather than a sneer. Some do read Barak's reluctance as a shadow over the account, and the text does note that the glory would go to a woman, Jael, which can be heard as an irony against the men. Grant all of that honestly. But notice what even that reading concedes, that God worked his deliverance through Deborah's leadership and Jael's hand, that the word of the Lord came through a woman and the nation followed it. Even the interpretation most cautious about her still has God speaking and saving through her. And the wider point stands regardless, because Deborah is one witness among many, and Huldah and Mary and Phoebe and Junia and Priscilla are not so easily read as rebukes to absent men. The aim is not to romanticize them but to stop erasing them, and reading them carefully is the opposite of erasing them.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Whose voice, telling you the truth about God, have you been slow to receive because of who was speaking, and what have you missed by it?
sessions.practice: This week, read the record for yourself rather than taking anyone's word for it, including this study's. Read Judges 4 and 5, Second Kings 22, Acts 18, John 20, and Romans 16, slowly, and let the women in them be as real and as honored as the text makes them. Write down what you notice that you were never taught, and ask honestly who decided you would not be taught it.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you spoke your word through Huldah and led your people through Deborah, you sent Mary to tell the men that death was beaten, and you moved Paul to honor Junia and Phoebe and Priscilla by name. Forgive your church where it learned to skip the pages you wrote, and forgive us where we have received the truth more slowly for the voice that carried it. Give us the honesty to read the whole of what you said, and the humility to be taught by whomever you choose to send. Let no daughter of yours grow up, as too many have, never once hearing the names of the women you honored. Amen.
reflection: Which of these women had I truly never been taught, and who chose the reading list that left them out?
Where do I read Scripture selectively, keeping the verses that confirm me and skipping the ones that complicate me?
Whose true word about God have I been slow to receive because of who was speaking, and what did the slowness cost me?
sessions.teaching: Bell says he could recite Paul's two hard sentences about women, the ones from First Timothy and First Corinthians, from memory before he was ten years old. He did not learn until he was a grown man, ordained, standing in pulpits, that the same apostle who wrote those sentences also ended his letter to the Romans by greeting a woman named Junia and calling her, in the same breath, notable among the apostles. The gap there is worth stopping over, because it is not a gap in the Bible. The Bible has always had both. The gap was in what he had been handed, in the reading list he had been given, in the verses that got underlined for him and the ones that got quietly turned past. So this session does something almost embarrassingly simple. It reads the pages the sermons skipped. Start in the Old Testament, because the omission runs all the way back. Deborah was a prophetess, and the text says plainly that she was judging Israel, sitting under her palm while the people came to her for judgment, which is to say she held the highest office in the land in that era, and when the time came for war the general Barak would not go without her. Huldah was a prophetess too, and when the lost book of the law was found in the temple and the king wanted to know whether it was truly the word of God, his officials did not go to Jeremiah, who was alive and prophesying nearby. They went to Huldah, and she authenticated the scroll, and the reformation of an entire nation ran through the word she spoke. These are not obscure figures buried in a genealogy. A judge over the nation. The prophet who launched a national reform. And most of us can name a dozen kings before we can name either of them. Come into the New Testament and the thread continues, right through the pages we know best without noticing what they say. Phoebe is named in Romans as a servant of her church, and the Greek word is diakonos, deacon, and she is almost certainly the one who carried the letter to the Romans across the sea and read it to them, which means the greatest theological document in the New Testament was first delivered by a woman. Priscilla, together with her husband Aquila, heard the eloquent preacher Apollos teaching what was incomplete, and took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately, and her name is listed first in that scene more often than not, which in that culture is not an accident. And then there is the morning that made all the rest possible. When Christ rose, the first witness was Mary Magdalene, and the risen Lord did not send her home to wait. He sent her to the men, to tell them he was alive, which is why the early church, long before our debates, called her the apostle to the apostles, the one sent to those who would be sent. Sit with how strange that is. In a culture where a woman's testimony was not accepted in a court of law, God arranged for the single most important announcement in the history of the world, that the tomb was empty and death was beaten, to come first from the mouth of a woman. No one fabricating a persuasive story would have written it that way. God wrote it that way on purpose. Now I have to be honest about what this session does and does not do, because the honesty is the whole point. It does not settle the debated questions about office and authority in the church. That is session four, and I will not smuggle the conclusion in here by piling up examples, because a pile of examples is not an argument about office, and to pretend it is would be the exact mirror image of the selective reading I am criticizing. Grant it plainly. None of this tells you by itself how to read First Timothy 2. But it settles something prior, and something the piling on cannot touch. It settles that God has spoken his word through women, led his people through women, entrusted the first news of the resurrection to a woman, and honored women by name at the very top of the church's founding generation. And it settles that a church which forgot to teach any of that, which could hand a ten-year-old boy two restrictive verses and not one of these names, was not being careful with Scripture. It was being careless with half of it. I know, because I was that boy, and then I was the man in the pulpit doing it again, and it took me far too long to read the pages I had been taught to skip.

scriptureStudy.note: Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time. The verb is plain and the office is the highest in the land in that age, so the text presents a woman leading the nation as a settled fact, not an apology it feels the need to make.

Barak said to her, if you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go. The general of Israel will not march without the prophetess, which the text records without embarrassment, letting her indispensability stand.

So Hilkiah the priest and the others went to Huldah the prophetess. When the king needs the lost law authenticated, his officials seek out a woman, and the reform of Josiah runs through the word she speaks, a national turning point routed through a prophetess.

Priscilla and Aquila took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately. A woman helps correct the theology of a gifted male preacher, and Luke records it as commendable, her name often listed first, without a hint that anything is out of place.

I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae. The word for servant is diakonos, deacon, and Paul asks the Romans to receive her and help her, marking her as a trusted leader and almost certainly the bearer of the letter itself.

Go to my brothers and say to them, I am ascending. Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples. The risen Christ makes a woman the first herald of the resurrection to the apostles, the reason the early church named her the apostle to the apostles.

And the twelve were with him, and also some women, who provided for them out of their means. Women funded and traveled with the ministry of Jesus, named individually, present at the center of the movement and not on its margins, easy to skip and impossible to justify skipping.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the history of the text itself, because the story of Junia is a case study in how an omission happens and worth a group's careful attention. For the first thousand years of the church the name in Romans 16:7 was read, without controversy, as Junia, a woman, and the great preacher John Chrysostom marveled in a homily that she should be called notable among the apostles, asking how great her devotion must have been to earn that title. Only later did the name begin to be rendered as a man's, Junias, a name for which there is essentially no evidence in the ancient world, and only in the modern period has careful scholarship, weighing the manuscripts and the accentuation, largely recovered the original reading of a woman. A group should sit with that, not to score a point but to see how a tradition can slowly edit its own Bible without meaning to, letting an assumption about what the text could not possibly say quietly reshape what it is allowed to say. Set beside this the honest scholarly debate that remains, whether Paul means Junia was well known to the apostles or counted among them, since the Greek can bear either and serious interpreters land on both sides, and a group should represent that debate fairly rather than seizing the reading that flatters its side. Then press the deeper and more uncomfortable question, which is not really about Junia at all. It is about the interpreter. We all come to Scripture with a prior sense of what it can be permitted to say, and that prior sense does its work most powerfully where we cannot feel it operating, in the verses we never think to question and the names we never think to check. The recovery of these women is finally an invitation to suspect our own reading, to ask where our tradition, our tribe, our comfort has been editing the text for us, and to submit even our most settled readings to the whole counsel of God rather than the portion we were handed. The aim is a group that reads more honestly, more suspicious of its own filters, more willing to be surprised by a Bible larger than the version it inherited.
sessions.caseStudy: A man in your group grows visibly uneasy as the session goes on, and finally says that all this feels like it is building toward an agenda, that he came for Bible study and it is starting to sound like a cause. He is not hostile, and he is not entirely wrong to be wary, because causes do sometimes wear Scripture as a costume. Here is the work for the leader, and it must honor his caution before it addresses it. His guard against bending the Bible to a movement is a good guard, and you should say so, because the study needs that instinct in the room, not banished from it. But turn the caution back on the actual question, gently, because the session has not added a thing to the Bible, it has only read parts of it aloud that he, like most of us, was not taught, and the wariness he feels may be less about an agenda in the room and more about how unfamiliar the plain text has been allowed to become. Ask him whether it is the study that has an agenda, or whether an older agenda decided long ago which verses he would hear and which he would not. Do not corner him or make him the example of a problem. Honor his love for the unbent Bible, and invite him to want the whole of it, Junia and Deborah included, precisely because he loves it unbent.

sessions.title: The Woman of Valor, Recovered
sessions.aim: To take the eshet chayil of Proverbs 31 back from the anxious checklist it became and return her to what the Hebrew actually says, a woman of valor, a strength word, so the passage stops functioning as a standard that crushes women and starts functioning as the tribute and blessing it was written to be.
sessions.summary: Bell says Proverbs 31 may be the most weaponized chapter in the Bible for women, quoted at bridal showers and Mother's Days as a to-do list so long that no living woman could finish it, rise before dawn, run a business, feed the household, clothe them all, never let her lamp go out, and somehow do it with a smile. Women have learned to dread the chapter that was written to honor them. The real question is what the passage actually is, because we have been reading it as a job description and it was never one. It opens by calling her an eshet chayil, and chayil is a warrior word, the word used for a mighty army and a valiant man, so the truest translation is not the perfect wife but the woman of valor, the woman of strength. And the poem is an acrostic, a formal Hebrew song of praise, each line beginning with the next letter of the alphabet, which is the structure of a tribute, not a checklist. It is closer to a medal citation than a performance review. Bell takes the strong case that the passage does set a high and even daunting bar, that its list of labors is real and can feel like a rebuke to a woman already drowning, and he grants the feeling honestly rather than waving it away. But the bar was never meant to be climbed alone and graded. The poem ends not on her achievements but on the one thing that holds them, that she is a woman who fears the Lord, and it puts praise in the mouths of her husband and children, which means the chapter is a blessing to be spoken over a woman, not a standard to be measured against her. Then the reversal. We turned a song of valor into an instrument of shame, a tribute into a taskmaster, and in doing so we did to Proverbs 31 exactly what session two said the church did to the whole Bible about women, we read it against them instead of for them. The woman of valor is not a woman who did everything. She is a woman worth singing about.

keyScripture.why: An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels. The word rendered excellent is chayil, valor, the same word used of armies and mighty men, opening the poem as a tribute to a woman of strength rather than a checklist of duties.

discussion.q: Bell says women have learned to dread the chapter that was written to honor them. If you are a woman, what has Proverbs 31 felt like when it was read at you, and if you are a man, how have you seen it used?
discussion.behind: Open on the felt experience, because for many women this passage carries real wounds. Let the room say honestly that the tribute has been received as an accusation, a bar too high to clear. Do not rush to fix it, and let the men hear how the chapter has actually landed on the women beside them before anyone reframes it.

discussion.q: The poem opens by calling her eshet chayil, a warrior word used for armies and mighty men, so the truest sense is woman of valor, not perfect wife. How does that one recovered word change the whole chapter for you?
discussion.behind: Put the recovered translation at the center. Chayil is strength and valor, not domestic competence, which shifts the passage from a standard of tasks to a tribute of character. Help the room feel the difference between being told to do everything and being called a woman of valor. The word is doing the heavy lifting, so let it.

discussion.q: Proverbs 31 is an acrostic, a formal Hebrew song of praise, which makes it closer to a medal citation than a performance review. What changes when you hear it as a tribute to be spoken over a woman rather than a list to measure her against?
discussion.behind: Press on the genre, because genre governs meaning. An acrostic tribute is not a job description, and reading it as one is a category error that turns a blessing into a burden. Help the room see that the chapter is meant to be sung over a woman, in the mouths of those who love her, not held up as the ruler she fails to reach.

discussion.q: Bell grants that the passage does set a high and daunting bar, and does not wave the feeling away. Where has a high biblical standard felt to you like a rebuke rather than a gift, and what do you do with that feeling?
discussion.behind: Hold the honesty that the bar is real. The reframe does not erase that the woman of Proverbs 31 does a great deal, and a woman already exhausted can feel accused. Do not resolve the tension too fast. Let the room name where Scripture's high calling has felt crushing, so the answer, that it is a tribute and not a graded test, actually meets the real ache.

discussion.q: Bell says we turned a song of valor into an instrument of shame, doing to this chapter what the church did to the whole Bible about women, reading it against them instead of for them. Where have you read Scripture against someone rather than for them?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication for everyone. The habit of turning a blessing into a bar is not unique to Proverbs 31, it is how a heart under law reads grace. Ask the room where they have wielded a good text as a weapon, against a spouse, a child, themselves. Go first, and keep it honest rather than performative.

objections.objection: You are just softening a hard passage to make women feel better. Proverbs 31 really does describe an incredibly accomplished woman, and pretending it is only a nice tribute dodges the challenge it sets.
objections.response: Grant the concern, because it guards something true, a refusal to dissolve every demanding text into a warm feeling, and that instinct keeps us honest. The woman of Proverbs 31 is indeed accomplished, and the poem does not hide her labor, and this study does not pretend otherwise. But changing the genre is not softening the passage, it is reading it correctly, and the two are not the same. An acrostic song of praise is a genuinely different kind of writing than a job description, and to call it a tribute is not to lower the bar but to name what the bar is for. The chapter holds up a woman of valor and says, look at her, she is worth everything, precisely so that such women would be seen and honored, not so that every other woman would be measured and found wanting. The challenge it sets is real, and it is the challenge of a whole life of strength and fear of the Lord, not the challenge of finishing an impossible daily list by bedtime.

objections.objection: If it is really about valor and fearing the Lord and not about the tasks, then why does the poem spend so many lines on her working, buying fields, making garments, running a household? You cannot just skip all that.
objections.response: You are right that we cannot skip it, and no honest reading should try. The poem does dwell on her work, her trading and planting and providing, and that is not decoration, it is the point, because valor in Proverbs is not an abstraction, it shows up in a life of competent, generous labor that blesses everyone around her. But notice what the work is doing in the poem. It is the evidence of her valor, not a quota assigned to the reader. The chapter is describing one particular woman being praised, the way you would describe the deeds of a person receiving an honor, and the deeds prove the character rather than prescribing a checklist for the audience. And notice where the poem finally rests, not on any of the tasks but on the fear of the Lord that gives them all their meaning, and on the praise of those who love her. The work matters enormously. It just is not a bar you clear alone to earn your worth, it is what a woman of valor's strength looks like when it is poured out in an actual life.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If the truest word over you is woman of valor rather than woman who did everything, whose voice have you let assign your worth by the length of your list instead?
sessions.practice: This week, if you are a woman, stop reading Proverbs 31 as your assignment and read it once as your blessing, out loud, letting the words be a tribute spoken over you rather than a bar held above you, and notice what resists. If you are a man, find a woman of valor in your actual life, a wife, a mother, a sister, a friend, and speak the tribute over her in your own words, naming her strength out loud rather than her tasks. Write down what it stirs to receive or to give the blessing instead of the burden.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you wrote a song to honor a woman of valor, and we turned it into a list to shame her with, taking a tribute you meant as a blessing and making it a bar no one could clear. Forgive us for reading your praise as a standard and your gift as a burden. Teach us to hear eshet chayil the way you wrote it, a woman of strength worth singing about, and put the song back in the mouths of the husbands and children who should be speaking it. To every woman here who has dreaded this chapter, let her hear it now for what it is, and let her rest in the one line that holds all the others, that a woman who fears you is to be praised. Amen.
reflection: What has Proverbs 31 felt like when it was read at me or used around me, a blessing or a bar, and why?
How does it change the chapter to hear eshet chayil as woman of valor, a warrior word, rather than perfect wife?
Where have I read a good and true text against someone, myself included, turning a blessing into a weapon of shame?
sessions.teaching: Bell says that if he had to name the most weaponized chapter in the Bible for women, he would not have to think long. It is Proverbs 31. It gets read at bridal showers and printed on Mother's Day cards and quoted from pulpits as though it were a job description handed down from heaven, and the description is long. She rises while it is still dark. She runs a business and buys a field and plants a vineyard. She feeds her household and clothes them in scarlet and keeps her lamp burning through the night, and she does all of it, apparently, without complaint and with strength for a smile. Women have learned to dread the chapter that was written to honor them, and I have watched it happen, watched a tired woman's face close a little when the reader announced the text, because she already knew she was about to be measured against a woman she could never be. So the real question is what this passage actually is, because we have been handing it to women as a checklist and it was never a checklist. Start with the very first word said about her, because the whole chapter turns on it. The poem calls her an eshet chayil, and chayil is not a soft or domestic word. It is a warrior word. It is the word used for a mighty army, for a valiant man, for strength and force and valor, the same word you would use of soldiers going out to battle. When our Bibles translate it excellent wife or virtuous woman, they are not wrong, but they are quiet about what the word is carrying, because the truest sense of eshet chayil is not the perfect wife. It is the woman of valor. The woman of strength. And that single recovered word changes the temperature of everything that follows, because now the labors are not items on a quota, they are the deeds of a warrior, the evidence of a valor that shows up in an actual life. Then look at how the poem is built, because the form tells you what kind of writing it is. Proverbs 31 is an acrostic. Each line begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to tav, all the way through, which is a deliberate and formal poetic structure, the shape of a composed song of praise. You do not write an acrostic to give someone their chores. You write an acrostic to honor someone, to sing them from A to Z, to build a tribute with the care of a poet. This chapter is far closer to a medal citation than to a performance review, closer to the words spoken over a person receiving an honor than to the standard they will be graded against. Now I have to grant the strong case honestly, because the reframe can be done cheaply and I do not want to do it cheaply. The passage does set a high bar. The woman in it does a great deal, and if you are a woman already drowning, already rising in the dark and working past the lamp-light and clothing a household, the last thing you need is a chapter that seems to say your best is a baseline. I will not wave that feeling away. The labor in the poem is real, and it can land like a rebuke on a woman who is already spending everything she has. But hear where the poem itself puts the weight, because it does not leave it on the tasks. It ends by lifting your eyes off the list entirely. Charm is deceitful and beauty is vain, it says, but a woman who fears the Lord is to be praised, which means the one thing holding the whole poem up is not her productivity but her God. And then it does the thing that settles the genre for good. It puts the praise in the mouths of her husband and her children. Her children rise up and call her blessed, her husband praises her. This is not a standard she is straining to meet. It is a blessing being spoken over her by the people who love her most. It is a tribute, sung, received, not a bar, raised, failed. So here is the reversal, and it is the same failure session two named, showing up again in a single chapter. We took a song of valor and made it an instrument of shame. We took a tribute God wrote to honor women and turned it into a taskmaster to accuse them. We read Proverbs 31 against women instead of for them, exactly the way the church read the whole Bible against them by skipping the ones it honored. The woman of valor is not a woman who did everything on a list. No such woman exists, and the poem was never asking for her. She is a woman of strength who feared the Lord and poured her life out and was, for all of it, worth singing about. That is what the chapter is. A song. It was always meant to be sung over women, not held over them.

scriptureStudy.note: An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels. The word for excellent is chayil, valor, a warrior term, opening the poem as a tribute to strength rather than a catalog of domestic duties, and setting her worth above jewels from the first line.

She dresses herself with strength and makes her arms strong. The imagery is deliberately physical and even martial, a woman girding herself as a warrior girds for battle, which confirms that chayil is not softened into mere tidiness but kept as genuine strength.

She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy. Her strength turns outward in mercy, so that valor in the poem is never self-serving competence but a power poured out for others, the shape love takes in a strong life.

Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come. Strength again, paired with dignity, and a fearlessness about the future, which is the portrait of a woman secure enough to laugh, not an anxious woman racing a checklist she can never finish.

Her children rise up and call her blessed, her husband also, and he praises her. The poem places the praise in the mouths of those who love her, which is the mark of a tribute spoken over a woman, not a standard measured against her.

Many women have done excellently, but you surpass them all. Excellently here is again chayil, valor, and the line honors many women of valor before singling out this one, so the poem celebrates a whole company of strong women, not a lone impossible ideal.

Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the Lord is to be praised. The poem lands its whole weight not on any task but on the fear of the Lord, naming the one thing that holds all the rest and the true ground of the praise.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the placement of the poem, because where it sits in the book is part of what it means and a group can miss it by reading the chapter alone. Proverbs opens by personifying wisdom as a woman, Lady Wisdom, who calls in the streets and builds her house and offers life to all who heed her, and the book closes with this portrait of the eshet chayil, so that the woman of valor at the end is, among other things, wisdom come down to earth and embodied in an actual life, the abstract virtue of the first chapters walking around in a real household. Read that way, the poem is less a standard for wives specifically and more a picture of what the wisdom the whole book commends looks like when it is lived, which is why some Jewish tradition sings it to a woman as a Sabbath honor rather than assigning it to her as a task. A group should weigh this against the checklist reading it likely inherited and ask what changed the tribute into a test. Set beside this the honest observation that the woman of the poem enjoys resources and standing many women never have, land to buy, servants to direct, capital to trade, and that reading her circumstances as a mandate would crush a woman without them, whereas reading her valor as the point honors the strength of a woman in far humbler conditions just as fully. Then take the harder turn toward the reader's own heart, because the deepest issue is not translation but the impulse that turns every good word into a bar. A heart shaped by law will hear even a blessing as a demand, will convert grace into pressure the moment it arrives, and Proverbs 31 has suffered under exactly that impulse, quoted to produce guilt in the very women it was written to honor. The aim is to let the group feel how the fear of the Lord, on which the poem rests, is itself the antidote to the anxious performance the poem got conscripted into, since a woman secure in the Lord she fears is precisely the one free to laugh at the time to come rather than race a list she can never complete.
sessions.caseStudy: A young mother in your group goes quiet when Proverbs 31 comes up, and when she finally speaks she says she stopped reading it years ago because it made her feel like a failure, that she cannot do a fraction of what that woman does and gave up trying. She is not looking for an argument, she is tired. Here is the work for the leader, and it must meet the exhaustion before it corrects the reading. Do not rush to tell her she has misunderstood the passage, because what she has actually received is the passage as it was handed to her, as a bar, and that reception was not her error alone but the church's. Sit first with the tiredness and honor it, because a woman drowning does not need another lecture on a text that has been used to drown her. Then, gently, offer her the recovered word, that eshet chayil means woman of valor and not woman who finished the list, and that the poem is a song meant to be sung over her, not a ruler held above her. Ask her whether she could bear to hear the chapter once as a blessing rather than a verdict. The goal is not to add Proverbs 31 back onto her load. It is to take it off her load and put it in the mouths of the people who should be singing it over her.
